- When sentiment is consistently positive (≥0.67) over recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast peaks, especially in early-to-mid horizon.
- When sentiment is negative (≤0.33) or volatile, model underestimates lows; increase forecast lows, especially in late horizon.
- Model often overshoots after sharp sentiment spikes (e.g., sentiment jumps to 1.00), leading to overvalued peaks — cap forecast peaks at 1.5x recent high or 1.2x prior 7-day average.
- Model exhibits mean reversion bias: over-forecasting in high-sentiment periods, under-forecasting in low-sentiment periods — adjust forecasts toward historical mean if sentiment shifts sharply.
- For 30-day horizon, model frequently overestimates early days (1–7) when sentiment is positive, then underestimates later days — apply “sentiment decay” correction: reduce forecast by 10–20% for days 8–15 if sentiment drops below 0.67.
- If sentiment history shows repeated low values (e.g., 0.00–0.33), model underestimates true lows — increase forecast by 15–30% for first 5 days of horizon if sentiment remains low.
- Avoid “sentiment echo” — if sentiment is high but price history shows no recent uptrend, don’t extrapolate; use 3–5 day moving average as baseline for forecast adjustment.
